submission.natural_language_explanation: The pole fires on the opening token of a multi-token lexical unit: the first piece of a word that GPT-2 splits into more than one token (Thunder|bolt, integ|rated, Sand|well, Fen|way, Ded|ication, G|MA, Sand|wich) or the first word of a compound noun, proper name or fixed collocation (wind turbines, Boston Red Sox, Chris Stapleton, Microsoft Windows, Internet Protocol, due to, come from, along with). It also fires on the lexemes that routinely fill that role even when no continuation follows (wind, sand, fire, water, ice, red, gold, glass, data, home, internet, Windows, Microsoft, Boston, Chris, come, came, due, along, up, through, East, and the word-initial fragments Gl/Med/Ins/Ind/inf), and it is near zero on ordinary words read as complete single tokens (stone, river, table, window, breeze, flame, London, John, Apple, Google) and on the non-initial pieces of multi-token words (well, ication, oure, way, bolt, which do not fire on their own).

Every spring the water in the valley rises. The people who live below the dam watch the gauge on the old wall and wait for word from the control room. If the level holds, nothing happens. If it does not, the road closes and the school sends the children home early. The dam is a long wall of concrete, grey and plain, with a walkway on top that nobody is allowed to use. Pine trees grow along both banks, and in a wet year the line where the water reached last spring is still visible as a dark band on the rock.

The first dam on this site was built by hand. Men came from the villages and worked for a season at a time, and the wages were enough to keep a family through the winter. They dug the channel with picks and carried the stone in carts. The wall they left behind was lower than the one that stands today, and it failed twice before the engineers gave up on it and started again from the base.

A modern dam is mostly a problem of getting rid of water. The spillway has to carry a flood far larger than anything the river has done in a hundred years, and it has to do so without the water digging out the ground below it. The gates have to open when they are told to open, in any weather, and they have to stay shut when they are told to stay shut. Every part of the system is checked twice a year, and the report goes to the regional office, where a clerk files it and rarely reads it.

The men and women who run the plant know the machine better than the people who designed it. They can tell from a sound in the hall whether a bearing is running dry, and they can tell from the colour of the water whether the intake is drawing silt. On a quiet night the hall is warm and loud and smells of oil, and the crew drinks bad coffee out of paper cups while the gauges tick over. In summer the foreman walks the length of the gallery every morning with a torch, checking for cracks in the lining and for water where there should be none. A crack the width of a hair is enough to bring the whole crew back at midnight, and nobody complains about it. The foreman has done the walk so many times that he knows where the paint is thin.

Last October a seal failed on the number two unit and the crew worked for fourteen hours to get it back online. By the time the relief shift arrived, the hydroelectric turbines had been turning for nine hours without a single fault, and the river below the dam ran clear for the first time in a week.
